Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Tafsir of Surat al-Mursalat (The Sent Forth)

It is Meccan.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah, both of whom said: It is Meccan, except for the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Bow down," they do not bow down﴾. Ibrahim related from al-Aswad, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "The surah al-Mursalat was revealed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) while we were with him on the mountain of Hira'. I took it fresh from the mouth of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a snake came out of its hole. We went after it, and it entered its hole. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'It has been spared your evil, just as you have been spared its evil.'"

And Allah knows best.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿By those [winds] sent forth in succession﴾. Most of the commentators said: it refers to the winds that are sent forth in succession, i.e., some of them follow others, like the mane of a horse (ʿurf al-faras).

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Hurairah, who both said: it refers to the angels who are sent with the ʿurf, i.e., the good (al-maʿruf).

And His saying: ﴿By the ones that blow violently, a blowing⁠﻿—﴾ [Q 77:2] refers to the winds, and their "'aṣf" (violent blowing) is the intensity of their blowing. It is said: "the wind 'aṣafat and a'ṣafat" when it intensified; this is what Ibn al-Sikkit said.

It is said: the winds are called ʿāṣifāt because they bring ʿaṣf, meaning the leaves of the crops.

It is also said: they are the angels, who drive away (lit. "shake/uproot") the souls of the disbelievers.

The Qur'an, 77:3: "And [by] those that spread [the clouds] far and wide."

And His saying: ﴿By those that spread far and wide﴾ — these are also the winds, which spread the clouds.

It has also been said: they are the angels, who spread the scrolls (ṣuḥuf) before the servants on the Day of Resurrection.

Abu Salih said: they are the rains, which cause the plants to spread (tanshuru al-nabat).

Al-A'sha said:

(If a dead man were leaned against her breast ...
he would live, and would not be carried to the grave.)

(Until people say, when they see it ...
"How wondrous, the dead man who has risen!")

And His words, ﴿Then those that separate, separating﴾ — according to most of the commentators (mufassirun), they are the angels, who bring the distinction (al-farq) between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful.

Qatadah said: They are the verses of the Qur'an, which distinguish between truth and falsehood, and between the lawful and the unlawful.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 77, verse 5:

And His saying: ﴿Then those who convey the reminder﴾ are the angels who convey the revelation to the prophets and messengers.

It is also said: they are the prophets. The first verse was explained in the same way, and it is like His saying: ﴿Then those who separate, separating﴾ in some of the views. And al-ilqa' (casting, conveying) is the throwing of one thing onto another, and in this context it means clarification and making understood. So the angels cast onto the prophets, the prophets cast onto the nations, and the scholars cast onto the learners.

And His saying: ﴿excuse or warning﴾. It is also read "ʿudhran" with the dhal pronounced with a sukun (ʿudhran).

Al-Farrāʾ said: "iʿdhāran aw indhāran" (as a giving of excuse or as a giving of warning).

It has also been said: "for the giving of excuse and warning."

Al-Ḥasan said: [God sends them] so that He may establish His excuse [against His creatures] by establishing the proof against them, and that He punishes them when they have become deserving of punishment by their denial after the proofs have been established.

Al-ʿudhr (excuse) is the manifestation of a meaning by which blame is removed from a person. This definition applies to creatures; as for God, it does not apply.

The accusative of "ʿudhran" is because it is a substitute (badal) for His saying "dhikran" (remembrance). It is as if He said: "fal-mulqiyāti ʿudhran aw nudhran" (then those who convey the reminder, as an excuse or a warning).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verse 7:

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is surely to occur﴾. Up to this point it was an oath.

And His statement: ﴿Indeed, what you are promised is surely to occur﴾ — upon this the oath falls.

It is said: Indeed Allah, may He be exalted, swore by these things, and He has the right to swear by whatever He wills of His creation.

It is also said: in the verses there is an ellipsis (idmar), and its meaning is: "By the Lord of those sent forth in succession (al-mursalat ʿurfan), and by the Lord of those that blow violently (al-ʿasifat ʿasfan)…" to the end of it, so that He has sworn by Himself.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So when the stars are obliterated﴾, meaning: effaced, and their light is extinguished.
And His saying: ﴿And when the heaven is split open﴾, meaning: it is cleft asunder.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 77, verse 10:

And His saying: ﴿And when the mountains are blown away﴾, meaning: they are uprooted from their places.

And His saying: ﴿And when the messengers are gathered at their appointed time﴾, meaning: they are assembled for their time, which is the Day of Resurrection, so that they may bear witness against the nations.

It has also been said: al-tawqit (appointing a time) is the determining of a time for the occurrence of an act. Since the messengers, peace be upon them, had been sent at known times in accordance with the welfare of the servants, they were appointed for all the times.

It is read: "wuqqitat," "wuqitat," and "uqitat," with one meaning. When the waw is pronounced with a ḍammah and the word begins with it, it is replaced by a hamzah. The Arabs say: wujuh and ajuh, and wijdanan and ajdanan.

It has also been said: "And when the messengers are appointed" means: they are given a term (ujjilat).

For what Day were they postponed?

And His saying: ﴿For what Day were they postponed?﴾ That is: For what Day were they delayed?
And His words: ﴿For a Day of Decision﴾ — meaning: they have been postponed until the Day of Decision, which is the Day of Resurrection.
And His saying: ﴿And what will make you know what the Day of Decision is?﴾ Al-Hasan said: By God, he did not know until God informed him.

And His saying: ﴿Woe on that Day to the deniers﴾. Al-Nu'man ibn Bashir said: "Wayl (woe) is a valley in Hell, in which there are various kinds of punishment."

This is also related from Ibn Mas'ud.

Almost. The Qur'anic quotation inside ﴿ ﴾ must be translated, and the passage is short, so I'll render it directly.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Did We not destroy the former peoples?﴾ That is: the people of Noah, ʿĀd, Thamūd, and those who were close to their time.
And His saying: ﴿Then We followed them with the later ones﴾. That is, those who came after them: Pharaoh, Haman, Qarun, and those after them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verses 18–19:

And His saying: ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals.﴾ That is: the polytheists of Makkah. We shall bring upon them the like of what befell them, because they have done the like of their deeds.

It is also said: "Then We shall follow them up with the later ones" refers to the disbelievers of Quraysh.

And His saying: ﴿Thus do We deal with the criminals.﴾ refers to those disbelievers who will come after them until the Day of Resurrection.

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Then We shall follow them up with the later ones" (sa-nutbi'uhum al-akhirin), and al-A'raj recited: "Then We follow them up" (nutbi'uhum) with the ayn vowelled with a jazm (sukun).

And His saying: ﴿Did We not create you from a despised fluid?﴾ Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatādah said: "weak."

And His saying: ﴿Then We placed him in a firm lodging﴾. ʿAṭāʾ, Ibn Jurayj and al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas said: it is the womb (al-raḥm), and the despised water (al-māʾ al-mahīn) is the drop of semen (al-nuṭfah).
And His saying: ﴿to a known measure﴾ means: until a known time, and this is a reference to the period of his remaining in the womb, in the mother's uterus.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verses 23–24:

His saying: ﴿So We determined, and excellent are the determiners.﴾ It is also recited as "fa-qaddarna" with the dal doubled (shaddah).

Al-Qutaybi said: The two are of one meaning. The Arabs say qadara and qaddara.

From this is his saying, peace be upon him: "If it is obscured for you, then determine for it" (fa-iqdurū lahu), meaning: determine for it.

(This statement has been objected to, and it was said: Had it been qadarna in the sense of qaddarna, he would have said) fa-ni'ma al-muqaddirun (excellent are the determiners).

The answer: He combined the two dialects. A poet said regarding something similar:

(And you denied me, though what you denied of the events was nothing but the grey hair and the bald head.)

It was also said regarding the difference between qadarna and qaddarna: with the light form, its meaning is "We ruled, so excellent are the rulers"; and the meaning of qaddarna with the doubled form is: We determined the creation of man through various stages: from a drop (nutfah), a clinging clot ('alaqah), a lump of flesh (mudghah), and what comes after that until We made him a complete human being.

It was also said: We determined (his being) wretched and happy, small and large, black and white, and other than that.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verse 25–26:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle?﴾ That is: kafitan (a gathering-place).

It was also said: a gathering (majma'an). So the kaft (kafat, "gathering-in") is the drawing together, and the meaning of kafat here is that the earth gathers the creation, living and dead. The gathering while alive is by their being contained and settled upon its back, and after death by their being contained in its belly, which is the graves. The cemetery of Baqi' al-Gharqad used to be called al-Kaftah.

And from Yahya ibn Sa'id and Rabi'ah: that clothing is cut when the shroud (kafan) is taken out, and also from the amulet (hirz). And he recited the Almighty's saying: ﴿Have We not made the earth a gathering-place for the living and the dead?﴾ Narrated by Sulayman ibn (Balayl).

And from al-Khalil ibn Ahmad: that the kaft is turning (taqallub).

And his saying: ﴿kafatan﴾ means: turning about (mutaqallaban).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verses 27–28:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We placed therein firm mountains, lofty ones﴾, meaning: elevated. It is said: "Shamakha Fulan bi-anfihi" (he lifted his nose, i.e., he raised his station/was proud) when he elevated his rank. Some of them said:

(When the free-born are my sons, and my station... and Khazim and the son of Khazim stand up for my affair.)

(I sneezed with a lofty nose, and my two hands reached the Pleiades, sitting, not standing.)

And His saying: ﴿And We gave you to drink sweet water﴾, meaning: sweet (fresh).

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The sources of sweet rivers are four: Jayhan, which is the river of Balkh; the Tigris and the Euphrates, for Kufa; and the Nile of Egypt.

Al-Kalbi mentioned that in this world there are three [rivers] from Paradise: the Tigris, the Euphrates, and the river Jordan. And the poet recited:

(When our Euphrates is absent from us, it is absent... and if it appears, one of its gifts and bounties is present.)

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verse 29:

Regarding His saying: ﴿Depart toward that which you used to deny.﴾ In the exegesis: people will stand at the heads of their graves for forty years when they are resurrected, the sun will be brought near their heads and its heat will be increased until great distress seizes them and until it takes hold of their breaths. Then Allah, exalted is He, will bring the believers, by His mercy, into a shade of His shade, while the disbelievers remain. A smoke from the Fire will come out for them and split into three branches, and it will be said to them: "Depart toward that smoke and seek shade in it." This is the meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Depart toward that which you used to deny.﴾ And He said: ﴿that which you used to deny﴾ because they used to deny the Fire.

And this is the smoke of the Fire.
And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Depart to a shadow of three branches﴾. It is what we mentioned, and it is an explanation of the first.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verse 31:

And His saying: ﴿[Neither] shade-giving﴾. The "ẓill" (shade) is a high screen that wards off the harm of heat from a person. So His saying ﴿neither shade-giving﴾ means: it does not ward off harm. It is in the form of a shade, but it does not have the meaning of shade.

And His saying: ﴿nor does it avail against the blaze﴾, meaning: it does not ward off from them the harm of the blaze, and "lahab" (blaze) is the flame of fire.

And from Qutrub, he said: "lahab" is thirst.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verse 32:

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, it throws up sparks﴾, meaning: sparks fly out from it.

And His saying: ﴿like a palace﴾. Abu 'Amr said: like a great building.

It was also said: like a tent of the tents of the Arabs, and the Arabs call such a thing a qasr (palace).

Ibn 'Abbas recited: "kal-qaṣar" with a fatha on the ṣad.

It was also said: they are the necks of palm trees.

It was said: they are the trunks of palm trees.

And it is related from some of them that it is a piece of wood which the people of the Jahiliyyah used to stack, about three cubits long, which they called the qasr.

And it is related from Mujahid that al-Qasr, with a sukun on the ṣad, is the mountain.

And it is related from Qatadah: the necks of beasts of burden, and it is with a fatha on the ṣad.

(And it is related from Ibn 'Abbas in one narration that it is the mooring ropes/cables of ships.)

It was also said: [the ropes of ships].

And it is related from al-Mubarrad (al-Mubarrad) that he said: it is the great, weighty portion of speeches.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verses 33–34:

And His saying: ﴿As if they were yellow camels﴾ means: black camels. The word jimalat (جمالات) is the plural of jamal (جمل), a camel.

It has also been said that it is a plural of a plural, as if they said jamal, jamal (جمال), and jimalat (جمالات), similar to their saying rijal (رجال), rijal (رِجَال), and rijalat (رجالات).

It was also recited with a dammah on the jim, making it jumal (جُمال).

And it was recited as jumalah (جُمَالَة) in the singular, like hajar (حجر) and hijarah (حجارة), and hamal (حمل) and hamalah (حمالة).

And His saying: ﴿Yellow﴾ means: black. He called them yellow only because a shade of black mixes with them, even though they are yellow.

From this comes the saying about the white gazelles: adam (أَدَم), because some turbidity mixes with them, even though they are white.

And the poet said:

(Those are my horses, some of them, and those are my riding camels... they are yellow (in their colours), like raisins.)

That is: black.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 77, verse 50:

And His saying: ﴿So in what statement after this will they believe?﴾ That is: in what book after the Qur'an will they believe, if they do not believe in this statement after its proofs have become manifest and the evidences have been established that it is from Allah? 

If someone says: What is the purpose of the repetition in His saying: ﴿Woe on that day to the deniers﴾ in this surah, when a single time would suffice for the meaning intended? The answer: We have already explained this in the commentary on Surah al-Rahman.

The reason for it is that when He repeated the mention of blessings in that surah, He repeated the rebuke against denying them and the prohibition of doing so with His saying: ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you both deny?﴾ And when He repeated the mention of the signs in this surah in order to establish proof against them, He repeated the mention of punishment upon them by mentioning "woe," so that it would be more forceful in warning and in leaving them without excuse. This is in accordance with the habit of Arabic speech, for a man says to another: "Have I not done good to you by doing such-and-such for you? Have I not done good to you by rescuing you from hardships? Have I not done good to you by interceding for you with so-and-so?" and other such things. Repetition is therefore fitting for him, because the things he establishes by it differ.

Muhalhil ibn Rabi'ah (Muhalhil ibn Rabi'a), lamenting his brother Kulayb, said in this sense:

(Upon me is that there is no fair dealing from Kulayb... when the base is driven away from the slaughtered camel)

(Upon me is that there is no fair dealing from Kulayb... when the neighbours of the protected one are wronged)

(Upon me is that there is no fair dealing from Kulayb... when the veiled women come out from their curtains)

(Upon me is that there is no fair dealing from Kulayb... on the morning of your great affliction)

(Upon me is that there is no fair dealing from Kulayb... when the protector of the one seeking refuge is wronged)

And Allah knows best.
